note: Third measure of all 144 quadruped mammals. Track: 20/141 unique heads before wave 7 · 52/144 after wave 13 · this run after waves 14+16. surfaceOnly is the pivot signal for the material pass.

rows.headWhy: Generic. The head is a small tan wedge with one dark round ear patch, a pale-iris eye and a stub muzzle — it is functionally the same head as the Cougar's in this batch, and swapping the two would go unnoticed. Nothing cat-specific is present: no broad rounded braincase, no wide zygomatic cheeks, no short foreshortened nose, no whisker field, and the clouded leopard's signature dark neck stripes and heavy jaw are absent. The 'ear' reads as a painted dark disc on the skull rather than a modelled round ear.
rows.topDefect: It is not a cat at all — a sheep/goat torso on straight hooved tube legs with a short curled stub tail, when the tail alone should equal the entire head-and-body length.

rows.headWhy: Generic. Round ear, large dark round eye, blunt short muzzle — this head is interchangeable with the Colugo's in this batch. The one defining coati feature, the long upturned rubbery snout that overhangs the lower jaw, is entirely missing; the muzzle is a short tapered cone no longer than the cougar's. The dark cap/mask tint is the only thing separating it from its neighbours, and tint is not shape.
rows.topDefect: The long upturned flexible snout — the single most identifying feature of a coati — is not rendered, and the tail hangs in a low curl instead of standing vertical like a flagpole.

rows.headWhy: Generic. Round ear, one dark-ringed eye, short tapered muzzle — the same head as the Coati's, at smaller scale. The reference calls for huge round forward-facing eyes filling much of the face; the rendered eye is small, lateral and no larger than the cow's. No forward binocular set, no oversized orbit, no shortened face.
rows.topDefect: There is no gliding membrane anywhere — the defining patagium spanning neck to fingertips to tail tip is absent, and the animal stands as an ordinary hooved quadruped instead of gliding.

rows.headWhy: Generic. A dark round ear disc, a pale yellow-green iris, and a short blunt muzzle on a small tan wedge skull — identical in construction to the Clouded Leopard's head beside it, and swappable with it without detection. The eye colour is the only differentiator. The mustRead black muzzle bars are not drawn, there are no cat cheek ruffs, and the skull is too narrow and too pointed at the nose for a puma.
rows.topDefect: The plain tawny coat is correctly unmarked, but the tail is a short upward curl instead of a very long heavy black-tipped rope, and the body is the shared lamb template rather than a deep-chested cat.

rows.headWhy: Specific, and the strongest head in the batch. The long boxy muzzle with a visible straight lip line and a defined nose pad reads unmistakably bovine, and the grey sideways-set ear over the crown is unlike any other head here. No other animal in this batch could wear it. Weaknesses: the ear reads as a flat grey chevron decal painted on the skull rather than a spooned volume with an inner surface, and there is no forehead poll or horn boss.
rows.topDefect: Two of the three mustReads are simply absent — there is no udder and no hanging throat dewlap — and the barrel does not sag, so the silhouette below the neck is still the batch's generic torso.

rows.headWhy: Weakly specific. The dark pointed ear and the longer, dark-masked snout do separate it from the round-eared cats and the coati, so a swap would be noticed. But the specificity is thin and partly broken: there is only ONE ear, and it sits so far forward on the crown and is so solid and conical that it reads as a horn rather than a large erect triangular pinna. The muzzle is not narrow enough for a canid, and there is no visible black nose pad terminating it.
rows.topDefect: The tail is a grey bristled fan splayed out sideways like a feather duster — neither bushy nor hanging low — and reads as a rendering artifact rather than an anatomical part.

rows.headWhy: Specific, but only by attachment. The branched sweeping antlers are correct and instantly identify the animal. Strip them and the head underneath is the same tan wedge with a stub muzzle used by the cougar and coati — no long cervine nasal bridge, no dark rhinarium, no preorbital gland. Worst of all, the mustRead 'large upright cupped ears' are effectively missing: only a tiny nub sits at the antler base where two big spoons should dominate the head.
rows.topDefect: The large upright cupped ears are absent, and the neck is short and thick where it should be long and thin, so the head sits on the shoulders instead of rising from them.

rows.headWhy: The head is pixel-for-pixel the Dog's head in a slightly cooler hue: same short wedge skull, same single dark triangular ear-mass fused to the crown, same white-sclera eye with round dark iris, same tapering snout with a pinprick nose and one lip notch. Nothing on it says canid rather than pony — no stop between forehead and muzzle, no cheek mass, no visible second ear, and the dark crown patch reads as a forelock. Swap it onto the Dog and no one could tell.
rows.topDefect: It is built on an equine chassis — deep barrel torso, straight columnar legs ending in dark hoof nubs instead of paws, no digitigrade hock, and a stiff bottle-brush tail stuck on above the rump — so it reads as a sandy pony, not a lean wolfish dingo (the white feet are also absent).

rows.headWhy: Identical construction to the Dingo's head — same wedge, same fused dark ear blob on the crown, same eye, same snout taper and nose dot. The mustRead's black nose is a tiny unpigmented tip, the ears are neither clearly erect nor clearly folded, and there is no jowl, brow or cheek to make it a dog's face. Interchangeable with the Dingo without detection.
rows.topDefect: Same horse body as the Dingo — barrel ribcage, hooved stick legs, and a bristly brush tail carried low off the rump rather than a plumed tail over the back — so the silhouette is a pony, not a mid-sized dog.

rows.headWhy: Within this batch the head is not swappable: the dark rounded ear mass plus the pale squared muzzle with a distinct lip line, chin and dark nostril marks belongs only to this animal here. But the specificity is carried almost entirely by the ear patch — strip it and the skull, the white-sclera eye with round iris, and the lip-and-chin muzzle are the same stamp used on the Camel, Eland and Duiker. The ears themselves are far too short and too round for a donkey; they read as bear or mouse ears, not the very long upright blades the reference calls for.
rows.topDefect: Two of the three mustRead traits are missing or wrong — the ears are stubby rounded pads instead of very long upright blades, and there is no short upright bristly mane at all (the neck crest is perfectly smooth); only the tip-tufted tail lands.

rows.headWhy: The down-hooked nose and drooping lower lip at the end of a narrow face, set under a dark brow patch with a barely-there ear, is specific enough that it could not be mistaken for the Donkey or Eland head in this batch. The camel read is helped by the long curved neck it sits on. Weaknesses: no split upper lip, no flared slit nostril, and the eye is the same generic white-sclera round-iris disc the whole batch shares — no heavy lashes or hooded lid.
rows.topDefect: The single hump is a separate smooth dome sitting on the spine with a visible seam where it meets the back, rather than a mass of the animal's own topline — and the reference's knobbly knee pads and splayed padded feet are absent, the legs ending in small dark hoof nubs like the horses in this batch.

rows.headWhy: The pair of small pale backswept spike horns over a very short blunt face is unique in this batch and cannot be swapped onto the Donkey, Camel or Eland. But the uniqueness is horn-borne: the underlying head is a shrunken copy of the shared wedge — same eye disc, same lip-and-chin muzzle — the forehead tuft between the horns does not read, and the ears are barely present behind the horns rather than the large cupped ears a forest duiker carries.
rows.topDefect: The diagnostic posture is missing — the back is essentially level with only a faint arch, so the hunched, rump-higher crouch that defines a duiker never reads; there is also an unexplained dark round blotch on the near haunch that looks like a rendering artifact rather than markings.

rows.headWhy: The long tightly-spiralled horns rising off the crown, with a small dark ear tucked below them, make this head unmistakable in the batch. Below the horns, though, it is the same generic ungulate face as the Donkey and Camel — identical white-sclera round-iris eye, identical straight muzzle with a thin lip line and small chin, no heavy jaw or broad blunt nose to suggest a half-ton antelope. Remove the horns and it swaps freely with the Donkey.
rows.topDefect: Two of the three mustRead traits are absent — there is no dewlap of loose skin under the throat (the neckline is a clean smooth curve) and no shoulder hump (the topline is flat), so the body is a mid-sized generic antelope rather than the massive ox-like frame the species requires.

rows.headWhy: Trunk, tusks and a large dark ear make this head unmistakable and unswappable. It is specific by prop, not by skull, and one prop is wrong: the eye is a big bright white-sclera disc with a round dark iris — the same eye stamped on the Dingo, Donkey and Eland — where the reference calls for a small eye, so the face reads cartoonishly wide-eyed. The domed forehead and temporal hollows of an elephant skull are not modelled.
rows.topDefect: The huge fan ear has detached from the head and sits as a flat dark teardrop pasted onto the shoulder, with a separate hard-edged angular plate jutting above it off the crown, so the head-to-body junction is anatomically broken; the trunk tip also has no grasping lips and the back shows no saddle dip.

rows.headWhy: The single most diagnostic aardvark feature — tall erect rabbit ears — is not drawn. Instead the crown carries one dark rounded flop cap, which is very nearly the same shape sitting on the Armadillo's head in this same batch; the pale tapered snout is likewise interchangeable with the Armadillo's. Swap the two heads and nobody would catch it. There is an eye with a pupil and a dark eye mask, and the snout does taper to a nose tip, but nothing on this head says aardvark rather than generic long-nosed digger.
rows.topDefect: The tall rabbit-like ears are missing entirely, replaced by a rounded dark flop cap, and the thick tapering kangaroo tail is instead a thin upward-curling hook on a flat-topped barrel with no arched back — three of the three mustReads fail.

rows.headWhy: Unmistakable: ground-reaching trunk, two curved tusks, a large eye with a visible iris and highlight, and a fan ear. No other head in this batch could stand in for it. What is still wrong is that the ear is placed and sized as a torso blanket — it begins at the eye and covers roughly half the body — so the skull itself has no readable boundary, no domed cranium and no cheek mass behind the trunk root; the head is inferred from the trunk rather than drawn.
rows.topDefect: The fan ear is mounted on the torso rather than the skull, swallowing the entire head-neck-shoulder junction so the head has no silhouette of its own, and the back arches convex where the reference calls for a saddle-shaped concave dip.

rows.headWhy: The huge rounded bat-like ear disc is genuinely specific and reads correctly at a glance — this head cannot be confused with any other in the batch. But the specificity is carried entirely by that one disc: the muzzle is a thin straight stick with no cheek mass, no chin and no depth to the jaw, and it is proportionally too small for the cranium. Cover the ear and the remaining head is generic.
rows.topDefect: The muzzle is a featureless thin stick with no jaw depth, cheek or chin, so the whole head hangs on the ear disc alone; the white-tipped brush tail also renders as a fan of straight straw spikes rather than fur mass.

rows.headWhy: The face is a small smooth pale wedge with an eye and highlight and a faint nose tip; the diagnostic camelid topknot fringe is absent and there is no split-lip or nose-pad reading on the muzzle. The ears are short dark nubs rather than the straight spear ears the reference calls for. Strip the long neck away and this head could be dropped onto the Arctic Fox with only the muzzle length changing.
rows.topDefect: The dense woolly fleece is drawn as radiating straight quills that break the silhouette into a hedgehog outline while the legs stay bare and smooth, so the animal's defining coat reads as spines rather than wool.

rows.headWhy: The lyre-shaped unbranched horns are correctly swept and clearly permanent horns rather than antlers, and they alone make this head unmistakable in the batch. Below them there is a real muzzle with a defined lip line, a nose and an ear at the horn base. The horns are drawn smooth, though — the ringing the reference specifies is not there — so the specificity is silhouette-only.
rows.topDefect: The torso is a uniform smooth tube with no deep chest and no tucked belly, with the shoulder and hip reading as two bolted-on ellipses, and the whole coat is turquoise rather than the tan flank and white belly.

rows.headWhy: Both of the head features that separate an arctic fox from any other canid are drawn backwards: the ears are pointed triangles instead of short and rounded, and the muzzle is long and slender instead of blunt and short. There is a good amber eye with an iris and a dark nose tip, but the result is a generic red-fox-shaped head painted white — take the ear disc off the African Wild Dog and the two heads are effectively the same object.
rows.topDefect: The two defining head traits are inverted — pointed ears and a long slender muzzle where the species requires short rounded ears and a blunt short muzzle — and the tail is a thin dark-striped bottlebrush instead of a dense round white one.

rows.headWhy: A tiny dark ear nub, a small eye and a short pointed snout on a smooth pale head — this is very close to the Aardvark's head in the same batch, and the two would swap without comment. Nothing armadillo-specific is present: no armoured head shield over the cranium, no small tubular ear structure, and the snout is neither long nor tubular.
rows.topDefect: The banded armour is a flat paint job — triangular chevrons airbrushed onto a smooth tube — with no raised bands, no carapace edge in the silhouette, no scute texture, and a smooth unringed tail that curls upward instead of tapering.

rows.headWhy: Specific: the branched backswept antler rack is unmistakable and nothing else in the batch could carry it, and the long tapering wedge muzzle with a darker nose tip, visible lip line and a small chin does read cervid. But subtract the antlers and the skull underneath is the same generic part the Fox uses — same tapering lozenge muzzle, same white-ringed cartoon eye. The eye is wrong for the family: a big white sclera ring around a dark pupil, where an elk shows a dark almond with no white at all, and the ear is a tiny dark nub lost at the antler base rather than the elk's large leaf-shaped ear.
rows.topDefect: The body is a stack of separately shaded blobs with visible seams — shoulder and haunch discs sit on the barrel like decals — carried on four jointless untapered slab legs, and the required cream rump patch is rendered as a DARK blob (inverted) with no shaggy neck mane and no tail.

rows.headWhy: The two ears are fused into one flat dark triangular plate continuous with the crown — no gap between them, no ear cup or inner-fur interior, no separate tip, no attachment point on the skull. So the head's whole silhouette is an anonymous dark wedge that reads closer to a bat or a hooded shape than to a fennec's twin outsize funnels, and the eye (small pale ring) and the short pale point of a muzzle are the same shared generic parts as the Fox and Fisher. Nothing but the wedge distinguishes it, and the wedge is not ear anatomy.
rows.topDefect: The tail is a radial spike-fan disc with a bright white ball at its tip mounted at the hip and pointing up and FORWARD over the back — the same generator artifact seen on Fisher and Fox — instead of a bushy black-tipped tail trailing behind.

rows.headWhy: Purely generic: a small dark rounded knob with a white-ringed eye and no resolvable muzzle beyond a slight bulge. The 'broad rounded ears' the family demands are not present as shapes at all — at most a faint bump on the crown. Swap this head onto the Fur Seal in this same batch and nobody would notice; the two are the same dark ball with the same ring eye. No nose pad, no nostril, no lip line, no cheek mass reads at render size.
rows.topDefect: The body is a straight ribbed cylinder with no shoulder or hip mass and no taper into the neck, on four identical stubby pegs, and the tail is the shared spike-fan brush ending in a glowing white ball rather than a dark tapering mustelid brush.

rows.headWhy: Specific and the best head in the batch: a large amber iris with a clear VERTICAL SLIT pupil set in a dark mask, a small rounded ear, and a short blunt muzzle on a round skull. The slit pupil is unique here and instantly reads felid — no other head in the batch could take it. Weakness: the head is very small relative to the body and the muzzle is a barely-modeled nub, so nose pad, nostrils and chin do not resolve; the ear is a plain rounded lump with no cup.
rows.topDefect: The body is a sheep, not a cat — roached arching back, deep narrow chest, four tall straight jointless legs ending in blunt caps with no paws, no tail, and the coat is a uniform dalmatian scatter of round dots rather than rows of solid spots with neck stripes.

rows.headWhy: Specific by construction: ground-reaching trunk, a pair of straight downward tusks, and a large rounded dark ear leaf — unswappable. But the head is undermined by parts: the eye is a big white-ringed cartoon eye on a species whose reference says eyes are SMALL, and it sits too high and too far forward with no brow dome or temporal hollow; the trunk joins the skull through a hard-edged pale rectangular strap that reads as a pasted plank, and the tusks emerge from that plank rather than from a lip line.
rows.topDefect: The trunk hangs BELOW the ground plane — it passes straight through the contact shadow and the foot line and floats off the bottom of the standing pose — while the legs are too slender and short to read as elephant columns.

rows.headWhy: Generic canid built from the shared parts kit: a tapering lozenge muzzle with a dark tip, a white-ringed eye, and two small dark ear triangles laid flat against the crown. Strip the antlers off the Elk in this same batch and you have the same head — same muzzle wedge, same ring eye, same construction. The ears are far too small and too short for a red fox (they should be tall, erect, black-backed, nearly a third of head height), and there is no cheek ruff, no white throat, no dark eye mask.
rows.topDefect: The proportions are a pony's, not a fox's — arched back, deep chest, four long straight legs, head carried high on a short neck — where the reference explicitly demands a body far lower and lighter than a dog's, and the tail is again the spike-fan with a white ball rather than a body-length white-tipped brush.

rows.headWhy: The most generic head here: a dark rounded knob with a white-ringed eye, a faint drawn smile for the mouth, and a dark round patch behind the eye that may be an intended ear but reads as a shading blotch. None of the three things that must read are present — no external ear FLAP standing off the skull, no whiskers, no protruding dog-like muzzle with a nose pad. It is interchangeable with the Fisher's head in this same batch.
rows.topDefect: It has no flippers at all — it stands on four short toed terrestrial legs, so the very long fore-flippers propping the chest up and the forward-rotated hind flippers that define a walking otariid are simply absent, leaving a plain ribbed barrel that could be any small mammal.

rows.headWhy: Within this batch the head is distinguishable — dark slate-grey head against the near-white body, a dark bandit-mask band through the eye, and two short pale horns — but the horns curve up and back like a generic goat's instead of the nilgai's short straight forward-pointing spikes, there is no throat beard tuft, and the muzzle is drawn as a long narrow wedge that projects like a beak rather than a bovid's deep blunt boxy muzzle.
rows.topDefect: The body is the batch's generic pale barrel-and-tube-legs mannequin — level-backed instead of sloping down from high shoulders, no slate blue-grey coat, no throat beard — so it is identical to the Oryx below the neck.

rows.headWhy: Nothing on this head is feline: it is a smooth tan dome with one flat circular ear disc pasted on top, a single large round eye, and a short rounded muzzle with a thin lip line — no cheek stripes at all (the reference's two black stripes per cheek are absent), no broad whisker pads, no wide-set forward-facing eye placement. Swap it with the Otter's head and nobody would notice.
rows.topDefect: It reads as a spotted sheep, not a cat — hoof-capped tube legs instead of paws, an ungulate barrel body, a thin stub tail, and blotchy scattered spots instead of chain-like rosettes streaking along the flank.

rows.headWhy: The two short knobbed ossicones on the crown are genuinely okapi-specific and appear nowhere else in the batch, and the dark chocolate head with a paler muzzle tip is right. But the ears are missing entirely — okapi ears are enormous and are the second thing you notice — and the pale stripes have been painted across the cheek and neck, which is anatomically wrong for the species.
rows.topDefect: The defining stripe pattern is in the wrong place — bold stripes cover the neck, shoulder and whole barrel while the hindquarters and upper legs (the only parts that should be striped) are plain, inverting the animal's one diagnostic marking.

rows.headWhy: The long ridged straight horns swept back over the neck are unmistakable and correctly drawn, which alone makes the head unswappable in this batch. What is still generic underneath them: the black facial mask has collapsed into two isolated black discs around the eyes, reading as goggles rather than a mask with a brow band, nose blaze and cheek bars, and the muzzle is the same narrow pale wedge used on the Nilgai and Pampas Fox.
rows.topDefect: The black leg markings are entirely absent and the body is the same slab-sided pale barrel as the Nilgai's, so nothing below the horns says oryx.

rows.headWhy: A small brown rounded blob with one round eye, one tiny round ear and a blunt short muzzle. The small ears and blunt snout are directionally right for a mustelid, but there is no broad flattened nose pad, no whisker field, no flat wide skull — it is interchangeable with the Ocelot's head at this size.
rows.topDefect: The tail is a thin curved string barely thicker than a leg, where the otter's single most defining feature is a thick muscular tail tapering from a base as deep as the hips.

rows.headWhy: The muzzle is the most pointed in the batch, which is the one right note, but the ear is a small dark nub barely clearing the skull instead of the large triangular ear the species is built around, and the rest is the same small grey wedge head with a dark eye patch used on the Nilgai. Strip the Nilgai's horns and the two heads are the same object.
rows.topDefect: The tail is a stiff radiating fan of bristles held out horizontally — it reads as a broom or a feather duster, not a long bushy dark-tipped tail carried low — and the body is an ungulate barrel on hoof-capped legs rather than a lean canid.

rows.headWhy: The round grey eye patch and the round ear on the crown do mark it as a panda within this batch, so it would not swap unnoticed. But the patches are grey rather than black and are plain circles rather than teardrops, only one eye patch reads clearly, and the head carries a long tapering snout with the nose at the tip — a generic ungulate muzzle grafted onto a bear, when the panda's muzzle is short, deep and blunt and the skull should be conspicuously round.
rows.topDefect: The black markings are laid out as two vertical belted-cow bands across the barrel while all four legs stay white, destroying the panda's actual pattern of a shoulder band running down into solid black forelegs.

rows.headWhy: Generic. A round dark ear disc, a blunt brown snout with an oval nose pad, and one oversized white-sclera cartoon eye — that is the same head the Hyrax in this batch wears, just scaled up. Nothing ursine-specific reads: no dished concave profile (the bridge is straight-to-slightly-convex), no broad flat brow, no small deep-set eye (the spec says small eyes and this one is the largest feature on the head), no heavy jowl. Swap it onto the Hyrax and only the size would give it away.
rows.topDefect: All three diagnostics fail at once — the topline is flat so there is no shoulder hump above the rump, the facial profile is not dished, and the front feet end in tiny dark nubs instead of long pale claws, leaving a generic brown ursine blob.

rows.headWhy: Specific, but only from the horns outward. The pale double-curve horns rising and splaying from the crown are unlike anything else in the batch, so a swap would be caught. The face underneath them is not doing the work: it is a short-to-medium antelope wedge, not the extremely long narrow tube a hartebeest needs, and the horns emerge from a vague dark smudge rather than the tall bony pedestal that is this animal's single most recognisable feature. Ear is a dark lump lost against the horn base rather than a readable long leaf.
rows.topDefect: The two skeletal signatures are absent — the face is nowhere near long enough and the horns sit on a smudge instead of a raised bony pedestal — while the back reads level rather than sloping steeply to the hindquarters, so the whole animal falls back to generic-antelope.

rows.headWhy: Specific in one respect: the muzzle is a heavy squared block that is genuinely wider and deeper than the cranium behind it, and no other head here has that mass — a swap would be noticed. But it is undercut badly. The eye is a large lateral white-sclera disc on the side of the face when the spec (and the animal) demands a tiny eye riding on top of the skull, the ears are essentially not present, and the nostrils are a single dark tip blob rather than a paired set on the muzzle's upper plane. The crown is also built from visible hard polygonal facets.
rows.topDefect: The body is a slim horizontal sausage on moderately long slim legs instead of an enormous barrel on stumpy pillars, so the one silhouette that makes a hippo a hippo is missing entirely.

rows.headWhy: Generic within this batch. The long tapering snout, the dark almond eye with a white catchlight, the single dark nostril dot at the tip and the dark triangular ear are the same geometry as the Hyena's head in this batch — put the two side by side and the only difference is the spot pattern painted over one of them. As an equine head in isolation it is passable, but it is not a head that could not be mistaken for its neighbour.
rows.topDefect: The crest mane along the arched neck is simply absent, and the tail is a straight bristle brush ending in a pale bulb blob rather than long flowing hair off a high dock — two of the three mustReads fail as structure, not as texture.

rows.headWhy: Generic — it is the Horse head from this same batch with spots on it. Same long slender tapering snout, same eye, same nostril dot. Worse, the ear is rendered as a small pointed dark triangle when a spotted hyena's defining ear is large and rounded, and there is no expanded zygomatic/cheek mass or deep jaw to carry the bone-crushing bite. The head reads canid-equine, not hyaenid.
rows.topDefect: This is the Horse asset recoloured and spotted — level topline instead of the skeletal steep slope from high shoulders to low hindquarters, pointed ears instead of large rounded ones, slender jaw instead of massive, and the identical bristle tail with the same pale bulb tip.

rows.headWhy: Generic. A small dark rounded blob with one small round ear, a white-sclera eye and a short blunt snout — the Grizzly's head at roughly 40% scale. The long whiskers the species is defined by are entirely absent, and there is no rodent-like upper lip or incisor hint. It is also visibly undersized against the stated head fraction, so it reads as a bolt-on knob rather than a head.
rows.topDefect: The head is both too small for the body and carries none of the species-specific features — no long whiskers at all — so a genuinely correct tailless rounded body is topped by an anonymous brown knob.

rows.headWhy: Specific enough to survive a swap: the pale horn curling around the side of the skull is unlike any other head here. But it is the wrong horn. It reads as a bighorn ram's tight forward curl, short and smooth, not the ibex's long massive scimitar arcing back over the shoulders, and there are no knobbed transverse ridges anywhere on it. The goat beard under the chin does not read as a distinct structure — it is lost in the general spiky fringe covering the whole animal.
rows.topDefect: The horns are a short smooth ram curl instead of massive knobbed backward-arcing ibex horns, and the shaggy coat is drawn as loose spikes protruding off the belly, back and flanks — detached strands breaking the silhouette rather than fur growing from it.

rows.headWhy: Unmistakable in this batch, but only because the horns are malformed: they render as a near-closed pale hoop that arcs DOWN across the muzzle and back up, occluding the face, instead of two horns rising and upcurving from the crown. The actual head furniture underneath is thin — a dark blob ear, no readable iris/pupil, and a muzzle that is a shaded lump with no distinct nose pad, lip line, or chin. Nothing here says bovine except the horn ring.
rows.topDefect: The horns form a closed ring passing in front of the face rather than two upcurving crown horns, which destroys both the head silhouette and the pale forehead patch it is supposed to frame.

rows.headWhy: The head is the same wedge, the same upright leaf ears, the same lyre horn pair, the same dark eye dot and dark nose smudge as the Gerenuk in this batch — put one head on the other body and nobody would notice. What identity it has (lyre horns, leaf ears) is exactly the part it shares.
rows.topDefect: The head is interchangeable with the Gerenuk's, and the shoulder/haunch read as pasted-on soft discs rather than muscle joined to the torso.

rows.headWhy: A direct visual duplicate of the Gazelle head at nearly the same scale — same lyre horns, same leaf ears, same eye and nose marks. The species' defining tiny wedge head with outsized ears and short hooked horns is not there; the head is too large relative to the neck and the ears are ordinary.
rows.topDefect: The head is a copy of the Gazelle's instead of the tiny huge-eared wedge that is the whole point of a gerenuk, so only the neck length distinguishes the two animals.

rows.headWhy: Distinct within this batch only in that it is the sole earless ball-head with a protruding snout — but the snout is a short duck-bill wedge that FLARES at the tip rather than a long tube tapering to a pin-hole mouth, the head reads as a round ball with a beak stuck on, the eye is a bare dot with no iris, and there is no ear at all. It reads more like a waterfowl head than an anteater's.
rows.topDefect: The snout is a short flaring beak on a round skull instead of the long tapered tube that defines the animal, and the tail is a broken-looking spray of straight bristles with a pale capsule intersecting it rather than a bushy flag.

rows.headWhy: Not confusable inside this batch (it is the only small carnivore head, with a round disc ear, a large round iris-and-pupil eye and a short blunt muzzle), but the head itself is a generic dome that any small mustelid or rodent could wear: no flattened crown, no whisker pads, no cheek mass, and the required cream throat bib is entirely absent.
rows.topDefect: The tail is a thin round tapering rope — the exact river-otter tail the reference note rules out — instead of a broad flattened paddle, and the stubby legs meet the smooth capsule body without shoulder or hip structure.

rows.headWhy: Clearly species-specific: paired dark skin-covered ossicones on the crown with small ears set beside them, a long tapering muzzle with a visible nostril and lip, and a large dark eye set high and far back on a patterned head. Could not be swapped with anything else here.
rows.topDefect: Anatomy reads correctly; what remains is surface — the coat is flat vector fill with hard-edged polygonal patches and airbrushed limb shading, with no hide grain, no soft patch borders, and a plastic sheen along the neck.

rows.headWhy: A pale featureless wedge with one dark ear blob; no backward-sweeping horns, no chin beard, no resolvable iris or nose pad. Strip the Gaur's horn hoop and the two heads are the same object in different colors — nothing in this head says goat.
rows.topDefect: All three identifying features are missing — no backward-sweeping horns, no chin beard, and the tail hangs down as a dark blob instead of flicking up — so the animal reads as a sheep, which the reference note explicitly warns against.

rows.headWhy: Specific only because of the black wire tufts — nothing else in the batch has them. Everything under the tufts is generic: the ear is a single broad brown cowl draped over the whole skull rather than two tall narrow pointed ears, the eye is a big pale ring with a dot (same cartoon ball as Caribou/Cattle), and the muzzle is the same snub tan wedge the Cheetah and Civet wear. Remove the tufts and this head is interchangeable with Chamois.
rows.topDefect: It is not built as a cat at all — barrel torso with a sagging belly on four straight pillar legs with dark hoof-like tips, no shoulder blade, no waist tuck, no digitigrade hock, so it reads as a small cream ungulate wearing cat ears.

rows.headWhy: Unmistakable in this batch: branched antlers with multiple tines and forward-pointing brow tines, a long pale tapering muzzle with a defined nose pad, and the shaggy throat fringe. No other head here comes close. The weakness is the eye — a big white-ringed googly ball sitting proud of the skull rather than a dark almond set into a socket.
rows.topDefect: The neck ruff is not a ruff — the same comb of hard straight spikes runs the entire spine, flank and belly from ears to tail, so the one feature that should localise to the throat is smeared over the whole animal.

rows.headWhy: Dark-on-dark: the ears do not break the silhouette at all, the top of the skull is a low rounded cap with no two upright triangles, and the muzzle/cheek/chin are invisible against the near-black head. The only thing carrying it is a single bright yellow slit eye. Delete that pixel and this head is an anonymous grey lump.
rows.topDefect: The warm-brown striped patch across the flank reads as a saddle blanket laid on top of a cold grey body — a hard-edged rectangular mat with combed strokes that clashes in hue with the coat and overhangs the belly contour, instead of tabby markings living in the fur.

rows.headWhy: Batch-specific thanks to the big pale horns sweeping laterally and back plus the dark brown eye mask. But the specificity is entirely in the accessory — the underlying head is the same narrow tan wedge as Chamois, and the defining bovine feature, a broad blunt square muzzle, is absent. The horn curve reads ram, not cow.
rows.topDefect: The mouth is broken — a pale grey wedge hangs off the end of the jaw looking like a detached lower lip, and the mouth line runs back far past where the commissure should sit.

rows.headWhy: A plain unmarked tan ungulate wedge. The black-and-white facial mask stripes that are the whole point of a chamois head are entirely missing, the eye is a small dark dot with no legible iris, and the horns splay up-and-forward in a V instead of standing vertical and hooking sharply back. Swap this head with Caracal's minus the tufts and nobody would notice.
rows.topDefect: Zero chamois identity on the head — no facial mask and wrong-shaped horns, leaving a generic tan goat.

rows.headWhy: Same construction as the Civet in this batch: rounded tan skull, one dark round ear disc at the top, snub muzzle, big round eye. The black tear stripes from eye to mouth — the single most recognisable cheetah head marking — are not present. The bright green-yellow iris is the only difference from the Civet's head, and that is a colour swap, not a shape.
rows.topDefect: The tail is a short thick stub curled up over the rump when a cheetah's is nearly body-length, thin and white-tipped, and the torso is a level sausage with no deep narrow chest or whippet waist.

rows.headWhy: Interchangeable with the Cheetah head: identical rounded tan skull, identical dark round ear, identical short snub muzzle. The two things that would make it a civet are both absent — the muzzle is snub instead of long and pointed, and the dark area around the eye is one soft blob rather than banded mask stripes.
rows.topDefect: The body proportions are inverted — long columnar legs holding a high, deep torso with a short upcurled tail, where a civet is low-slung on short legs with a long trailing ringed tail, so it reads as the Cheetah recoloured.

rows.headWhy: Specific only by the pale lyre horns curving out then up plus a dark eye mask around a white-ringed eye — that is enough that swapping it with Kudu or Jackal would be noticed. Everything else is generic: the long leaf ears are absent (nothing projects from the skull), and the muzzle is the same drooping tube used on Kudu, ending in a hooked bulb with a small pink mouth. The horns carry the whole identity.
rows.topDefect: The diagnostic long leaf ears are missing entirely and the muzzle droops into a hooked bulb, so the head is carried by horns alone, while the rump has neither the vertical black stripes nor the white patch and the hocks have no black tufts.

rows.headWhy: The only species signal is a single dark pointed triangle ear; strip that and this head is interchangeable with the Kinkajou's — same taper, same small white eye with a dot pupil, same short blunt muzzle tube, same head-to-neck join. The slender fox-like muzzle called for is not there: no tapering nose bridge, no dark nose, no facial mask, no cheek ruff.
rows.topDefect: The whole animal reads as a pony — arched equine back, thick neck, four long straight legs ending in dark hooves, and a brush tail with a pale tip carried up — instead of a light, leggy, low-tailed canid.

rows.headWhy: This head is pixel-for-pixel the same construction as the Leopard's in this batch: identical large circular ear disc pasted flat on the side of the skull, identical oversized eye with a bright ring, identical short rounded snout. Swapping them would be invisible. The jaguar's defining massive broad blocky jaw, heavy cheek mass and short deep muzzle are entirely absent — the skull is small and round, closer to a lemur than a big cat.
rows.topDefect: It is not built as a cat at all — a barrel torso on four short straight hoof-tipped legs with a thin rat tail — and its head is indistinguishable from the Leopard's in the same batch.

rows.headWhy: Generic. The round ear disc is the only differentiator from the Jackal head, and the rest matches it exactly: a projecting blunt muzzle tube, a small white eye with a dot pupil, no cheek mass. The brief calls for a round teddy-bear face with huge dark eyes; the render has a long-snouted face with a small pale eye, which is the opposite reading.
rows.topDefect: It is drawn as a slender long-legged hoofed quadruped with a short thick curled tail, when a kinkajou is a compact woolly arboreal carnivoran whose long prehensile tail should be roughly body length.

rows.headWhy: Strongly specific and unmistakable in this batch: two enormous round fringed ears set wide and low on a broad flat face, a very large black spoon-shaped nose pad dominating the muzzle, and two tiny beady eyes set close above it. No other head here could be mistaken for it or substituted into it.
rows.topDefect: It does not actually grip the trunk — the body floats in front of the log with paw shapes resting on its own belly rather than forelimbs wrapping the bole with claws — and the limbs stay unresolved lumps.

rows.headWhy: Specific: tall pale corkscrew horns with visible twists plus dark chevron banding across the muzzle and a pale nose band make it unswappable with the Impala's smooth lyre horns. Still incomplete though — the enormous rounded satellite-dish ears are not present, only a small dark lobe behind the eye, so the single most recognisable non-horn kudu feature is missing.
rows.topDefect: The flank striping renders as a dense black scribbled brush mass hanging off the shoulder and past the belly line instead of 6-10 thin clean white vertical stripes, and it reads as damage on the coat.

rows.headWhy: Identical to the Jaguar head in this same batch — same flat circular ear disc, same oversized bright-ringed eye, same short rounded snout on a small skull. A swap would be undetectable. Nothing distinguishes the leopard's narrower, finer skull from the jaguar's heavy one.
rows.topDefect: Body and head are the Jaguar render reused — a chunky short-legged hoof-tipped barrel with a short thin tail — so neither the low-slung slender cat build nor the tail nearly as long as the body exists.

rows.headWhy: It is the Brown Bear's head in a different palette: same ovoid skull, same single round ear disc stamped on the crown, same white/amber ring eye, same forward wedge muzzle with a nose pad, lip curl and chin. Nothing distinguishes ursine from the Bobcat's head either except scale. The reference's diagnostic straight facial profile is not expressed (the profile is a generic convex dome), the muzzle is grey rather than tan, and the ear is nearly invisible because it is the same near-black as the skull it sits on.
rows.topDefect: It does not read as a bear at all - a light-grey sheep-barrel body on straight cylinder legs ending in dark pointed hoof-like tips, with no plantigrade paws, no claws, and a level back instead of the required rump-higher-than-shoulders line.

rows.headWhy: Generic. The head is a small tan wedge with one dark round ear disc, an amber dot eye and a short nose - the same construction kit as both bears, just shrunk. Not one felid cue survives: no black ear tufts, no cheek ruff or whiskers, no short broad cat face, and the pupil is an undifferentiated dot rather than a readable slit at this size.
rows.topDefect: The whole animal is a spotted lamb - deep barrel torso, upright straight legs with hoof-like dark tips instead of digitigrade paws - so the leopard-spot pattern is doing all the identification work while the skeleton says ungulate.

rows.headWhy: Specific, but entirely on the strength of the horns: two long pale spiralled S-curve horns plus dark stripe marks running onto the cheek make this head unmistakable within the batch. Strip the horns and what remains is the same tapered herbivore wedge as the Bull and Camel. The leaf ear is present at the horn base, but there is no white chevron between the eyes, and the eye is a cartoon white ring with a black dot rather than an antelope's dark almond.
rows.topDefect: The horns stand almost straight up with a forward tip curl instead of sweeping heavily back over the neck, and the flank stripes render as dark brown on chestnut - the polarity is inverted from the required white stripes, and mid-back they collapse into one solid smeared slab.

rows.headWhy: Interchangeable with the Black Bear's head - identical skull ovoid, crown-mounted round ear, oversized white-sclera eye, identical forward muzzle wedge. The reference's dished concave face and broad forehead are absent; the profile is convex like every other head here. Worse, a pale angular prong hangs below the muzzle reading as a protruding tusk or lower canine, which no bear has.
rows.topDefect: The feet are dark pointed hoof tips on tapered cylinder legs - the long straight pale digging claws that are this species' single most diagnostic feature are entirely missing, and the shoulder hump is only a faint rise rather than a muscular mass.

rows.headWhy: Distinctive within the batch because of the horn geometry - one pale crescent sweeping over the crown and a large C-hook curling down and back up - but the anatomy behind it is wrong. There is no fused helmet boss across the forehead; the two horns are separate and the down-hooking one is drawn in front of the muzzle rather than beside the cheek, so it crosses the face. The large fringed drooping ears that should hang below the horns are not there, and the eye is almost lost under the upper horn.
rows.topDefect: The C-shaped horn is planted over the front of the muzzle instead of beside the cheek and there is no forehead boss, so the head reads as a ram or warthog rather than a Cape buffalo.

rows.headWhy: Readable as bovine and separable from Buffalo and Bongo by its two short pale upward crescent horns and the dark mask patch around the eye - but only by the horns. The muzzle itself is the same narrow tapered wedge the Camel uses, where a bull needs a broad blunt square muzzle with a large flat nose pad; and the eye is the same white-ring cartoon eye shared across the batch, so no species pupil is legible.
rows.topDefect: Two of three mustRead features are missing - there is no pendulous dewlap under the throat at all, and the shoulder mass is a flat dark colour patch with a hard straight polygon edge rather than an actual humped neck silhouette.

rows.headWhy: The long raised neck sells the camel, but the head on the end of it is generic: a tapered wedge with a big grey-blue ring eye and a small nose, essentially the Bull's head with the horns deleted. None of the camel-specific facial anatomy is present - no split protruding upper lip, no slit nostrils, no heavy overhanging brow with lashes - and no ear is drawn anywhere on the skull, which reads as an omission rather than a deliberate hidden-ear treatment.
rows.topDefect: The hump is a separate lighter dome dropped on top of the back with a visible seam where it meets the body instead of flowing out of the spine, and the legs are far too short - the leg mass is well under half the total height against a body that sits low and heavy.

rows.headWhy: Specific only because of paint: the crown and the round ear carry stripe strokes and the eye is a warm amber iris with a narrow pupil. The underlying head is a flat rectangular block with a bulge tacked on the front — no cheek ruff, no brow spots, and the muzzle is a featureless wedge with a single dark dot for a nose, no lip line, no chin. Strip the stripes off and it is the Weasel's head enlarged.
rows.topDefect: The stripes are painted inside a hard-edged rectangular patch that stops in mid-flank and mid-shoulder instead of wrapping the body contour, and the tail is a short boneless stub with no rings.

rows.headWhy: The paired downward tusks make it unmistakable in this batch, but they are the ONLY specific thing — they sprout from the side of the cheek, well above the mouth line, rather than descending from the upper jaw behind the lip. Under them the head is a generic canine box: an oversized cartoon eye with a big white sclera (the row calls for small eyes), a round dark button nose, a simple smile line, and a small circular mark where a walrus has no external ear at all. No bristle mass whatsoever.
rows.topDefect: The dense bristle moustache — the single most identifying feature of a walrus muzzle — is entirely absent, leaving a smooth dog snout with tusks glued to it.

rows.headWhy: This head and the Wild Boar's are the same object with a different tint: identical rounded-box skull, identical dark triangular ear patch in the same spot, identical large white-sclera eye, identical small pink nose disc, and the identical pair of straight white spikes rising off the top of the snout. Nothing flat-fronted or wedge-like, no facial warts, no long warthog face.
rows.topDefect: The head is interchangeable with the Wild Boar's, and the tusks emerge as straight spikes from the upper snout beside the eye instead of curving up out of the jaw.

rows.headWhy: Only the horns identify it, and they are malformed — a pale closed crescent ring floats across the cheek and over the muzzle like a wreath, with a second arc crossing behind, rather than two horns rooted at the skull and sweeping back. The head beneath is a small generic bovid wedge: tiny eye, two small dark triangle ears, and no broad wet muzzle pad — the nose end is narrow and dry with no visible nostrils.
rows.topDefect: The signature swept-back crescent horns render as a closed pale ring floating in front of the face, unattached to any readable horn base on the skull.

rows.headWhy: Completely generic: a small tan rounded lump with one round ear, a dot eye and a blunt snub nose. No long slender mustelid snout, no dark nose pad, no whisker field, no dark eye mask or facial contrast. Swap it onto the Tiger with the stripes removed and nobody would notice.
rows.topDefect: The animal has no tail at all — the long tube body simply ends at the rump — and the short legs render as hollow cylinders with visible open elliptical end caps.

rows.headWhy: Distinct in this batch thanks to the long tubular equine muzzle with a squared end and a visible nostril mark. But the ears fail: instead of two very long upright ears there is one fused dark ovoid mass sitting on the crown like a hood, with no second ear separated from it. There is also an unresolved step/notch where the muzzle joins the skull, so the face reads as two parts pushed together rather than one head.
rows.topDefect: The very long upright ears — the species' defining feature — are collapsed into a single dark blob on top of the head, and the erect mane along the neck is missing.

rows.headWhy: Identical construction to the Warthog: same box skull, same dark eye patch, same big white-sclera eye, same pink nose disc, same two straight white spikes off the top of the snout. Nothing boar-specific — no long tapering snout, no small deep-set eye, no heavy jowl.
rows.topDefect: The bristly coat is a rectangular patch of straw-like strokes that spray off the silhouette on all four sides — including below the belly and behind the rump — instead of a mane along the spine, and the back is level with no shoulder hump.

rows.headWhy: The bandit mask has collapsed into a single soft grey bruise smeared around the one visible eye — it does not read as a band spanning both eyes, and it has no white brow band above or white cheek below to bound it. Strip that smudge and the head is the exact same kit as the River Otter's in this batch: same pale rounded dome, same small round ear placed at the back of the crown, same short blunt taper to a dot nose, same white eyeball with a dark disc. Nothing in the skull, ear, or muzzle shape says raccoon.
rows.topDefect: The animal is a featureless near-white barrel with a dead-flat back — no hunched arch with the rump above the shoulders, no grizzled dark coat, no long-fingered plantigrade hands — so the three short tail bands are the only thing carrying the ID.

rows.headWhy: Genuinely specific: two dark-backed pointed triangular ears set wide on the crown and a long narrow wedge muzzle tapering to a dark nose — no other head in this batch has that combination, and a swap would be spotted instantly. Weaknesses that remain are within the head: the muzzle is a flat two-dimensional wedge with no cheek mass or jawline behind it, and there is no white throat/cheek patch to break the uniform orange.
rows.topDefect: The body is a small horse, not a fox — deep chest, high withers, long straight pillar legs, a level back — and the brush tail is rendered as a flat splayed fan of separated bristles like a broom head rather than a thick cylindrical plume.

rows.headWhy: Every head-defining marking is missing: no white face mask, no rust tear-stripes running down from the eyes, no white-rimmed ears. What is left is a dark maroon cap sitting on a pale rounded muzzle — literally the Raccoon head with a different colour hat on it. Nothing about the skull, the single round ear, or the stub muzzle distinguishes it from the other small carnivores here.
rows.topDefect: All three signature reads fail at once — no white face mask with tear-stripes, no jet-black legs and belly (the legs are the same salmon as the body), and no pale rings on the tail — while the silhouette is the same long-legged pony body used for the Red Fox, so it reads deer-sized rather than raccoon-sized.

rows.headWhy: Unique in the batch, but only because of the antlers — they are the sole identifying element. The face beneath them is a plain tapering tube: a small dark eye with a catchlight, a nose dot, a soft chin, and ears so small they are nearly lost at the antler bases. Remove the antlers and this head is interchangeable with the Saiga's minus its nose.
rows.topDefect: The antlers are generic upright branched deer forks with tines going up and back — there is no forward-sweeping palmate brow shovel projecting over the face, which is the one thing that separates reindeer antlers from every other deer's — and the neck carries no thick pale mane.

rows.headWhy: The paired pale horns make it unmistakable in this batch, but they are drawn as two ivory tusks angled forward off the side of the snout rather than as a dominant nasal horn rising off the top of the nose bridge with a smaller one behind it. The eye is the bigger head problem: it is large, round, and glossy with a bright catchlight, sitting where a small deep-set rhino eye should be far back on the side of the skull. The dark rounded shape at the crown is a generic blob, not the tall cupped tubular ear.
rows.topDefect: The hide is a smooth featureless grey with no plating and none of the deep shoulder and flank folds called for, so with its oversized bright eye and forward tusks the head reads as a hippo or pig rather than a rhino.

rows.headWhy: Completely generic — a small pale dome with one small round ear, a faint grey ring around a white eyeball, and a short blunt taper to a nose dot. There are no whiskers, no broad flattened otter skull, no wide fleshy nose pad, no visible lip shape. Paint the Raccoon's mask onto it and it would pass as the Raccoon; it is the same head geometry.
rows.topDefect: The tail is a thin rope-like whip curving off the rump instead of the thick muscular base tapering to a point, and the feet are smooth rounded stubs with no toes and no webbing at all.

rows.headWhy: The most specific head in the batch by a wide margin: a genuinely bulbous pale snout mass overhanging and drooping past the mouth line, paired with two straight vertical horns carrying visible horizontal ring annulations. Neither element appears anywhere else here. The remaining head weakness is the abrupt head-to-neck junction with no throat or jaw mass, and the dark hooked mouth line hanging below the muzzle reads as a detached mark rather than a lip.
rows.topDefect: The legs are pin-straight identical cylinders front and rear with no stifle, hock, or fetlock articulation, and the torso is a single undifferentiated barrel with a soft airbrushed disc pasted on the haunch.

rows.headWhy: Specific: the full radiating mane ring, a gold iris with a true vertical slit pupil, a broad snub muzzle with a black nose pad and whisker lines — nothing else in the batch could wear this head. But the specificity is almost entirely the mane; the skull under it is the same rounded dome the mustelids use, and the single ear is a flat dark disc pasted at eye level with no cup, rim or tragus.
rows.topDefect: The ear is a flat circular cutout sitting beside the eye rather than a cupped round ear on top of the skull, and the mouth is a cartoon smile curve with no jawline, so the face under the mane is not built like a cat's.

rows.headWhy: Specific: the only long tapered camelid wedge in the batch, high-set eye, stalk neck. But the ears fail the read — two short rounded lobes that read as a clover/flower, not long banana curves — and the mouth is drawn as a grey L-shaped bar with a hook at the tip that looks like a metal clasp rather than a split camelid lip; no nostril, no chin.
rows.topDefect: The muzzle terminates in a hooked grey mechanical-looking lip bar instead of a nose pad with nostrils and a split lip, and the ears are short nubs where the species' whole silhouette cue is long banana ears.

rows.headWhy: Specific only because of one cue: a triangular ear capped with a black tuft spray, plus a gold eye. Everything else is generic — the muzzle is a long narrow tapered snout closer to the Maned Wolf's than to a cat's short broad face, the flared facial ruff is entirely absent, the cheek/chin mass reads as flat, the second ear is missing, and a flat quadrilateral flap juts out behind the ear as a polygon artifact. The pupil is round here while the Lion's is a slit, so the cat-family pupil rule is not even applied consistently.
rows.topDefect: Two of the three mustReads are missing outright — no flared facial ruff and no oversized snowshoe paws (feet are the same blunt tube stubs as every other animal here) — so the render reads as a spotted goat with a tuft.

rows.headWhy: Specific: long orange muzzle with a black nose pad at the tip, a big white-ringed round eye, and a dark cap running back into the nape mane. But the ear is a single solid dark triangle with no inner surface and no second ear, sized like a witch's hat, and it fuses with the mane into one crest that reads as a pterosaur fin rather than two large erect ears.
rows.topDefect: The defining proportion is gone — the legs are ordinary quadruped length with no black stockings instead of stilts at ~60% of standing height, while an oversized squirrel-like tail plume is bolted to the hip.

rows.headWhy: Generic. It is the identical head build used on Marten and Meerkat: rounded dome skull, a flat dark round ear disc set high and hard against the eye, a white-ringed dark eye, a short tapered muzzle with a tiny nose dot and a small mouth curve. Only the tan palette differs. No orange incisors, no blunt rodent skull, no rodent ear (small, low, half-buried in fur).
rows.topDefect: None of the three species cues exist — no large orange incisors, no long scaly rope tail (the tail is a short thin upward curl), no webbed hind feet — so this is an unnamed small carnivore, not a muskrat/coypu.

rows.headWhy: Generic. Head-for-head interchangeable with Marsh Rodent and Meerkat: same dome skull, same flat disc ear jammed against the eye, same white-ringed eye, same short tapered muzzle and mouth curve, differing only in brown tint. The ear is a disc, not the large rounded ear the row asks for, and the pale orange throat bib that would separate it from its neighbours is absent.
rows.topDefect: The head is a recoloured clone of the Marsh Rodent and Meerkat heads, and the orange throat bib — the one marking that would break the tie — is not drawn.

rows.headWhy: Generic. Third copy of the same head as Marsh Rodent and Marten — dome skull, flat dark ear disc high on the crown pressed against the eye, white-ringed eye, short tapered muzzle with a nose dot. The dark rings around the eyes read as ordinary head shading merging into the ear disc, and the ears are high crown discs rather than small ears set low on the sides.
rows.topDefect: It is drawn as a horizontal four-legged animal wider than it is tall, when the species is defined by the bolt-upright sentinel stance propped on hind legs and tail (row asks aspect 0.5, upright).

rows.headWhy: Side-by-side with Wild Pony this is the same head asset at ~90% scale: identical two-tone dark triangle sitting centrally on the skull (one 'ear', and it overlaps the top of the eye), identical white-sclera googly eyeball with a plain black pupil and no visible iris ring, identical hooked nostril mark drawn high on the bridge, and the identical tan lip bar. Nothing on it is Przewalski-specific — no erect brush mane on the crest, no dark mask, no pale mealy muzzle. Swap the two heads and no one would know.
rows.topDefect: The muzzle 'lip' renders as a hard-edged tan stick that projects past the nose tip into empty space with a knob on the end, so the face terminates in a floating prop rather than a nose pad with nostrils.

rows.headWhy: The pink nose disc with two dark nostril pits is genuinely species-specific and nothing else in the batch has it — that one element alone makes the head unswappable. Everything around it is generic though: the eye is the same white googly ball as the horse and pony, the 'ear' is a ragged dark chevron with a notch bitten out of it that reads as a rendering artifact rather than a pig ear, and the head is a rounded lozenge, not the long wedge the row calls for. The disc is also pasted flat onto the side-facing plane instead of capping the snout end.
rows.topDefect: No shoulder hump and no tusks — the topline is dead level and the only thing near the mouth is the same floating lip bar the horse has, angled down and back where an upward tusk should be.

rows.headWhy: Direct duplicate of the Wild Horse head — same central dark ear triangle, same white googly eye, same nostril hook, same projecting lip bar, only slightly shorter in the muzzle. The row's distinguishing feature, a thick shaggy forelock falling over the eyes, is absent: the shaggy fringe is drawn on the neck and barrel behind the head, and the forehead is bare. Broad-forehead read is also missing.
rows.topDefect: Its head is a rescaled copy of the Wild Horse's, so the one place the two species must diverge is the one place they are identical.

rows.headWhy: The head itself is a featureless cream lump: no ear, no nose pad, no nostril, no lip, and the eye is a tiny smudged dark bean with no iris and no pupil at all — the eye pass did not land here. Its only identifying mark is the horn, and that horn is the same flat pale crescent ring the Wildebeest wears, just recolored. Swap the two heads and the difference reads as a palette change.
rows.topDefect: The horn is a flat untextured crescent with no spiral, no ridging and no taper, and it is drawn on top of the face so it occludes the eye and the entire muzzle instead of curling beside the head.

rows.headWhy: The amber iris with a hard vertical slit pupil is the single most convincing feature in the batch and it is unmistakably feline — not swappable with anything here. But it is carrying the whole head alone: behind it sits a large flat brown disc that reads as a second eye or an open ear canal, the actual ear is a notched grey tab further back, the muzzle is a stub with no nose pad, and a detached black wedge floats below the jawline.
rows.topDefect: It stands on the horse's leg kit — four straight unjointed tubes with dark hoof-shaped tips, no paws, no hock or elbow — so a cat's head is bolted to an ungulate body.

rows.headWhy: The horn is the same flat pale crescent asset as the Wild Sheep's, drawn over the front of the face, and it hides the eye entirely — there is no eye, iris or pupil visible on this animal at all. What remains is a grey box muzzle plus a few dark bars, which is close enough to the sheep's silhouette that the two heads differ mainly in tint. No chin beard on the head.
rows.topDefect: The shaggy mane is drawn as long dark streaks across the mid-barrel and flank rather than on the neck and dewlap, so the defining wildebeest feature lands in the wrong place on the body.

rows.headWhy: Not swappable — the long thin tapering snout with a small dark bead nose and an amber round-pupil iris exists nowhere else in the batch. But it is unique for the wrong reason: the snout is a narrow tube with no jaw depth and no lower-jaw mass, so it reads bird or anteater, not the broad blocky canid head the row demands. The ear is the same single dark triangle asset the horse, pony and pig wear, placed centrally on the crown instead of two erect triangles set at the sides.
rows.topDefect: It is wearing the horse's body kit — the same bristle-fan tail with a pale club tip carried high off the rump, and four straight tube legs ending in dark hoof tips instead of paws.

rows.headWhy: The head is dominated by one enormous flat ring-disc (a round ear scaled to eclipse the entire skull) with a small tan inner circle; the actual face is a tiny pale wedge peeking out to the right carrying a single yellow vertical-slit eye and one black nostril dot. This is the identical construction to the Serval in this batch, differing only in tint and coat spots — swap them and nobody could tell. No second ear, no cranium, no cheek mass, no chin, and nothing of the broad flattened low-wide-eared sand cat skull the row asks for.
rows.topDefect: A single giant disc-ear is pasted over the skull so the head has no cranium at all, only a tiny muzzle wedge protruding from behind it.

rows.headWhy: Big white-ringed round eye with a round pupil, an oval nose pad stuck on the side of the face like a decal well away from the lip, a thin hooked lip stroke, and a jagged sawtooth notch chewing the back of the skull. The two brown blobs above the eye are a smear, not an external ear flap. This exact head appears on the Seal and Sea Otter in this batch; only the fill colour changes.
rows.topDefect: There are no long fore-flippers lifting the chest — the body is a smooth extruded cylinder on four stubby paddles, capped at the rear by a flat pipe-cut disc, and the head is the same part the Seal wears.

rows.headWhy: Same round white-ringed eye, same side-stuck oval nose pad, same hooked lip stroke as the Seal and Sea Lion, with two small dark bars over the brow. The blunt round face is roughly the right mass, but it carries not one whisker despite whiskers being the species' signature, and the body's spiky fur fringe stabs across the jaw and cheek instead of resolving into a face.
rows.topDefect: It is drawn standing on four legs like the Seal and Sea Lion rather than floating belly-up, so the one posture that identifies a sea otter is absent.

rows.headWhy: Identical build to the Sea Lion and Sea Otter heads — round ringed eye, side-mounted oval nose pad, thin hooked lip, sawtooth notch at the rear of the skull — and worse, it carries two grey discs above the eye that read as ear flaps on the one animal in this batch defined by having none.
rows.topDefect: It is propped up on four limbs like a sea lion instead of lying on its belly with hind flippers trailing back, which by the row's own note makes it the wrong pinniped.

rows.headWhy: The most specific head here: a long tapered dark snout with a faint nostril and lip line, a horizontal-oval eye with a tan iris and dark pupil, and two pale horns rising off the brow. Nothing else in the batch could pass for it. But the horns are a forward-curving V of banana shapes rather than short straight backswept spikes, the large donkey-like ears the row calls for are simply missing, and stray grey fringe strokes are drawn across the muzzle and jaw.
rows.topDefect: The head has no ears at all, and the horns curve forward off the brow instead of running back as straight spikes off the skull top.

rows.headWhy: A carbon copy of the Sand Cat head: one oversized flat ring-disc swallowing the skull, a tan inner circle, and a small pale muzzle wedge with a yellow vertical-slit eye and a nostril dot. The very large upright oval ears that are the serval's single defining trait are nowhere — instead there is one round disc, the wrong shape and the wrong count.
rows.topDefect: The defining tall oval ears are replaced by the same single flat disc worn by the Sand Cat, so the head is neither a serval's nor unique.

rows.headWhy: A curl horn distinguishes it inside this batch, but only by accident: the curl is a fat cream ribbon in exactly the same colour as the face, looping across and over the front of the head where it covers the eye socket and part of the muzzle, so it reads as rope lying on the face rather than horn growing off the skull. Under it the face is a generic pale block with a small dark eye set high on the brow and two nub ears; nothing about it is narrow or bare.
rows.topDefect: The horn curl is drawn in the face's own colour and laid flat across the front of the head, obscuring the eye and muzzle instead of coiling behind the ear.

rows.headWhy: The head is built from the same three parts as the Wombat's in this batch and would swap with it unnoticed: a flat circular ear decal pasted on the skull (a disc with an inner disc, no pinna depth or canal), an oversized round eye with iris, round pupil and a big white catchlight, and a smoothly tapering snout whose 'nose' is a single dark comma with no pad. Nothing wolverine-specific is present — no broad blunt black rhinarium, no dark facial mask, no pale forehead/cheek band, no wide low-set skull. The eye is also far too large for the 'small eyes' spec.
rows.topDefect: Every leg ends in an angle-cut hollow cylinder with a dark elliptical hole where the paw should be — no foot, no toes, no claws — on an animal whose mustRead is 'huge clawed paws'.

rows.headWhy: Same template as the Wolverine: flat round ear disc, huge round eye with catchlight, tapered muzzle ending in a small dark bean nose with one nostril, a shallow lip line and a soft chin. The one feature that would make it a wombat — the broad bare blunt rhinarium filling the end of a squared-off snout — is absent, so the head is a generic small-mammal head that reads slightly cuter than the Wolverine's and nothing more.
rows.topDefect: The defining broad bare-nosed blunt snout is missing (the muzzle tapers to a small bean nose) and the 'short powerful bowed digging legs' are straight thin pegs ending in rounded blobs with no claws.

rows.headWhy: Unique in this batch, but only because of the horns, and they are malformed: the near horn is a flat cream ribbon bent into an almost closed ring that is drawn ON TOP of the face, crossing the cheek and muzzle rather than growing out of a boss on the skull. The ear is a lumpy cream mass fused into the horn base and unreadable as an ear. The eye is a dark almond with a sliver of amber, almost entirely occluded by the horn ring. The muzzle mass is broad and bovine, which is right, but the lip, nose pad and mouth line are buried under the horn overlay.
rows.topDefect: The horn is a flat ring painted over the front of the face — it occludes the eye and crosses the muzzle instead of attaching to the skull — and the ear is fused into it.

rows.headWhy: Distinguishable in this batch only by the long equid wedge silhouette — no zebra information is on it. The face is a blank unstriped white slab (the body stripes stop at the neck), there is no dark muzzle, no forelock, no erect mane reaching the poll. The ear is a hard-edged grey triangle placed at eye level and drawn OVER the eyeball. The eye is a round-pupil bead, not the horizontal bar an equid should carry. The nostril is a thin 'c' outline with no pad, and the mouth is a straight grey rectangular bar with a machined shoulder that reads as a tool clamped to the muzzle, not a lip. Against any other horse-shaped head it would be indistinguishable.
rows.topDefect: The ear is a flat opaque triangle sitting on top of the eye socket, and the mouth is a rectangular machined bar instead of a lip.

rows.headWhy: It is the same head kit as the Mongoose in this batch with the hue turned down: identical flat dark round ear-disc pasted on the top-rear of the skull, identical oversized white-sclera eye with amber iris and round pupil at the same offset, identical short wedge muzzle with one nostril dot and the same upcurved lip line, identical neck taper. Swap the two heads and only the brown value changes. Nothing about it says mustelid - the eye is a big lemur orb where a mink's should be a small dark bead, and the promised white chin patch is not there (only a general pale throat).
rows.topDefect: The head is a hue-shifted duplicate of the Mongoose head, and the tail is a fan of straight spikes ending in a stray white dot rather than a thick tapering furred tail.

rows.headWhy: The long forward-projecting cylindrical snout with a blunt rounded tip and a terminal nostril dot is not confusable with anything else in the batch, and the earless skull reads correctly. But it is specific by silhouette only: the snout is a grey tube stepped onto the head with a visible join seam rather than a pink fleshy cone continuous with the face, and there is a clearly visible dark eye with a white catchlight on the side of the head, which the species must not have.
rows.topDefect: The forelimbs are ordinary tapering hoof-tipped legs set back under the chest, so the single most diagnostic mole feature - huge outward-turned spade digging hands beside the head - is absent entirely.

rows.headWhy: Interchangeable with the Mink head: same round ear-disc, same big white-ringed eye with round pupil in the same socket position, same wedge muzzle with a single nostril and the same lip curve, same neck. The snout is a touch longer, which is the only differentiator, and it is not enough to survive a swap. It carries no mongoose-specific cue - no small low-set rounded ear tucked against the skull, no dark eye mask, no pointed pale-tipped face.
rows.topDefect: The head is the Mink head recoloured, and the animal stands on long upright legs like a small dog instead of reading as a very long low tubular body on short legs.

rows.headWhy: Unmistakable in this batch thanks to the palmate antlers and the long deep muzzle - but unique for the wrong reasons. The antler palms are flat 2D lens shapes with four straight stick tines and they are mounted at eye level, crossing in front of the face so no eye is visible at all. A hard-edged white/silver ring sits on the forehead at the antler junction like a monocle. The nose is a small dark dot high on the bridge instead of the big bulbous overhanging moose nose, and the lip is a long straight dark bar ruled back across the cheek.
rows.topDefect: The antler palms attach at eye level and cover the face - hiding the eye completely - and a stray hard silver ring is drawn on the forehead between them.

rows.headWhy: The pale curved dagger horns over a long white wedge muzzle with a throat fringe is not swappable with any other head here. Specific but still wrong in the details: the two horns straddle the eye, the front one erupting from the brow ahead of the socket instead of both rising from behind it; they are cream rather than black; the eye is an amber orb sitting on the crown at the horn base rather than on the side of the face; the ear is a barely-legible grey lobe lost behind the horns; and the beard reads as a dirty grey spike fringe on the throat rather than a white chin beard.
rows.topDefect: One horn springs from in front of the eye so the pair straddles the socket, and the eye itself is set on the crown rather than on the side of the face.

rows.headWhy: Distinct in-batch because of the large pink nose disc, but it is specific to the wrong animal - it reads as a pig, not a tapir: a rigid barrel muzzle ending in a flat mauve disc with two drilled nostrils, no short mobile proboscis overhanging the lower lip, and no white lip rim. Two hard black triangular wedges sit on the cheek in front of and below the eye where no feature belongs, which looks like an ear drawn at the wrong anchor. The eye is the same oversized bright amber orb used on the Mountain Goat.
rows.topDefect: The snout terminates in a flat pig-style nose disc instead of a short flexible overhanging proboscis, and two unexplained black wedges are stamped on the cheek in front of the eye.

rows.headWhy: Unique only because of a malformed artifact: the horns are a uniform-width cream tube that loops into a near-closed circle lying across the middle of the face, crossing the muzzle and covering the eye region, with a second hook over the crown. There is no boss - no broad horn plate meeting across the forehead - and no taper from thick base to thin tip. The muzzle behind it is a blunt box with a hard vertical seam where it meets the head, and the eye is only readable as a dark slit half-buried under the horn loop.
rows.topDefect: The horns are a constant-thickness ring laid over the face with no forehead boss and no down-and-out hook beside the cheeks.

rows.headWhy: Specific: a small skull with a long, thin, tapering conical snout, a single pinprick nostril at the tip, and no ear at all — nothing else in the batch reads like it, and the hidden-ear choice is right for a pangolin. What is still wrong on the head: the snout is a separate uniform-width tube butt-joined to the cranium with a visible hard seam rather than tapering out of the skull, and the eye is a large mammalian ball with a bright specular highlight, far too prominent for the 'small eyes' spec.
rows.topDefect: The tail is a short, thin, unscaled, uniform-width tube curling upward off the rump instead of a thick tapering scaled tail as long as the whole body.

rows.headWhy: Generic: this is the Pig's head recolored grey. Same large round nose disc with two dark nostrils, same dark two-pointed wedge ear notched into the forehead with no visible base, same round pale iris with a highlight, same straight grey lip rod along the mouthline, same absent chin. The one feature that should separate it — straight downward tusks — is instead two thin grey sticks projecting forward along the mouth, so nothing head-side distinguishes it from the Pig except hue.
rows.topDefect: The tusks are two thin grey rods projecting forward along the mouthline rather than straight-down tusks rooted in the jaw, so the peccary's only identifying feature fails to read.

rows.headWhy: The flat round pink snout disc and forward-flop ear are the correct pig read, but the identical construction is used on the Peccary in this same batch — same nose disc, same notched dark wedge ear, same eye, same grey lip rod — so the two heads are interchangeable once you set colour aside. Two further head problems in the pixels: the nose disc is inset from the snout tip so the muzzle mass continues forward past it, and the grey lip rod projects out beyond the snout silhouette into empty space.
rows.topDefect: The curly corkscrew tail is entirely absent — the rump instead carries a hard-edged flat maroon disc with no blend into the hide.

rows.headWhy: Distinct in the batch by silhouette: a small narrow white head with a long, straight, slightly convex muzzle ending in a black nose set right at the tip, carried on a long neck — no other head here has that proportion. But the ear is broken: it is two overlapping flat grey-mauve discs pasted on the forehead, oversized and reading as a lens artifact, not a small round furred ear. The back of the cranium also has a machined stair-step notch in the silhouette, and the grey lip rod runs out past the jaw as a straight stick with a square cap.
rows.topDefect: The ear is two overlapping flat grey discs stuck on the forehead instead of a small round furred ear, and the same flat-disc primitive is punched into the white rump as a conspicuous hard-edged grey circle.
