rows.headWhy: Generic: the head is built from the same parts as the Quoll's in this batch — a large opaque dark round ear-cap that covers the entire cranium and encloses the eye, one big round pale eye, and a short muzzle tapering to a dot nose. Only the cream-vs-brown tint separates them. It also misses its own spec twice: the ears should be thin and bare, not a solid dome helmet, and the nose should be pink, not a small dark dot.
rows.topDefect: The prehensile tail is a short, smooth, body-coloured tube instead of a long naked scaly rat tail, and the legs terminate in open hollow cylinders with visible dark interiors rather than feet.

rows.headWhy: Specific: the forked horns — a vertical shaft with a short forward prong on each — are unmistakable and nothing else in the batch carries them. Still wrong: the horn shaft and its basal band are layered over the eye so the eye is partly occluded by its own headgear; the eye itself is a silver ball with a specular dot rather than an iris with a pupil; and the dark ear is buried behind the horns. Below the horns the muzzle is a generic ungulate taper with the same straight grey lip rod seen on the Pig, Peccary and Polar Bear, projecting past the jaw on both sides.
rows.topDefect: The horn shaft is drawn in front of the eye rather than behind it, and the rump carries a flat dark-brown disc exactly where the pronghorn's signature white rump patch belongs (the white throat bands are also missing).

rows.headWhy: Generic: the same head as the Possum — a big dark round ear-cap sitting over the whole cranium, one large round pale eye with a dark pupil, and a short muzzle tapering to a tiny dark dot nose. Swap the two heads and only the brown-vs-cream tint gives it away. The required pink pointed snout is absent; the snout is the same brown as the rest of the face.
rows.topDefect: The spotting is inverted — black blotches on a pale cream back instead of white spots on dark fur — and it stops dead at the rump instead of continuing onto the tail, which is itself a stiff radiating fan of identical bristle spikes rather than a bushy tail.

rows.headWhy: Specific — the banded, forward-curling trunk with a single-lipped tip and the short tusks are unmistakable and belong to nothing else in the batch. But the face still wears the shared generic muzzle kit: a grey oval nose pad and a straight dark bar for a lip pasted onto the cheek where an elephant has neither, since its nostrils live at the trunk tip. The ear fails outright — it is a hard-edged dark-grey slab with a straight vertical leading edge and a squared top, sized at roughly a quarter of the body and planted on the shoulder well behind and below the eye, so it reads as a saddle blanket rather than the small triangle the species needs. The forehead is one smooth dome with no twin-dome dip. The eye is a brown iris in a hard pale annulus that reads as a printed button, and it is far too large for the 'small eyes' the row calls for.
rows.topDefect: The ear is an oversized hard-edged rectangular slab sitting on the shoulder instead of a small triangle behind the eye.

rows.headWhy: Generic. It is the same long tapering herbivore wedge as the Bison head in this batch — same bulbous cranium narrowing to a blunt rounded snout, same oversized eye inside a bold white ring, same hairline-thin straight bar for a lip running most of the jaw and terminating in a tiny hooked nostril tick, same small dark leaf ear crowding the eye. Recolor one into the other and nobody would notice. Nothing camelid is present: no split upper lip, no closable slit nostril, no shaggy cheek or throat hair, and the eye sits up on the brow ridge rather than on the side of the skull.
rows.topDefect: The two humps are separate stuck-on domes resting on a dead-flat slab topline with a visible seam beneath them, so they read as loaves set on a table rather than as mass rising out of the back.

rows.headWhy: Specific enough that a swap would be caught — the narrow pointed mustelid snout plus dark facial bars appear on no other head here. But the markings are built wrong in two ways: the coloration is inverted (a pale grey face crossed by dark brown bars, where a badger is a dark face carrying a white stripe), and the bars run diagonally down across the muzzle like cracks or war paint instead of one stripe running front-to-back over the crown. A solid black blob sits behind the eye and reads as a hole punched through the cheek rather than an eye patch. The ear is a small grey rounded rectangle lying flat on the skull with a machined straight edge, and the snout simply ends with no nose pad at all.
rows.topDefect: The flank is a full-length dark horizontal bar with dozens of dark spikes hanging off it — a comb, not a badger's pelage — while the actual white facial stripe is missing and a black void sits in the cheek.

rows.headWhy: Unique only because of the horns, and they are the defect. Instead of smooth crescents sweeping out and up from the poll, a pair of thick pale bands loops down and forward across the face, meeting in a lumpy knot between the eyes, with one arm curling across the cheek and jaw and the other passing directly over the eye and hiding it almost completely. It reads as a pretzel or a rope halter laid on the face; nothing attaches to the skull. Take the horns away and what remains is the same brown wedge as the Bison, with dark pointed ear leaves and a blocky dark nose carrying a straight-cut rectangular edge on the muzzle. The white band above the muzzle called for by the row is not readable — the muzzle is uniformly dark brown.
rows.topDefect: The horns are a pale pretzel-shaped loop draped down the front of the face, unattached to the poll and covering the eye.

rows.headWhy: The most convincing head in the batch — a broad cranium, a genuinely small rounded ear set on top of the skull, a muzzle that tapers into a round dark nose pad, a curved lip line and a cheek mass. It reads ursine and would not pass as any other animal here, though the muzzle is a touch long and canine for a brown bear and the head is not dished. Two build faults remain: the muzzle is a lighter panel with a visibly straight vertical seam down its side and a straight bottom edge, so a rectangle is showing through the face, and the eye is a bare white ring with a black dot in it — no lid, no brow, no socket, floating on the cheek. The cheek 'fur' is a fan of short pale dashes that reads as scratches.
rows.topDefect: The legs are literal flat rectangles — parallel sides, square corners jammed into the body, no taper or joint — ending in oval shadow pads with a row of five white blocks for claws.

rows.headWhy: Generic. There are no orange chisel incisors anywhere — the single feature that makes a beaver head a beaver head is absent, leaving a snub muzzle with a tiny nose lump and a thin downturned line for a mouth. The ear is a flat dark capsule smudged onto the forehead above and behind the eye, with no bowl, rim or attachment; it reads as a bruise. The eye is the same white-ringed button used on the Camel and Badger. What is left is a plain rounded brown head that could be moved onto any small mammal in this batch without comment.
rows.topDefect: The defining orange chisel incisors are entirely missing, and the hind legs terminate in open-ended tubes whose flat elliptical cut faces are visible where feet should be.

rows.headWhy: It is the Bactrian Camel head recolored. Same narrow wedge tapering to a blunt snout, same oversized white-ringed eye high on the brow, same thin bar lip ending in a hooked nostril tick, same small dark ear leaves — and it is carried high on an upright neck, the opposite of a bison's posture. There are no horns at all; the dark shapes above the eye are ears, not horn bases. There is no beard, only a few stray dark strands dangling below the jaw that read as loose hairs. None of the bison's massive, broad, heavy low-slung skull is present.
rows.topDefect: No horns, no beard and no shoulder hump — the topline is flat and actually rises toward the hips, giving exactly the uniform cow barrel the reference note warned against.

rows.headWhy: Unique in this batch, but specific to the wrong animal: the ears are a single large dark triangular cone sitting centrally on the crown (not a pair of tall rounded-triangular hyena ears), and the muzzle is a long needle-thin wedge tapering to a pinpoint nose pad with a hairline lip running its whole length. There is no cheek mass and the lower jaw is a thin sliver with no chin. The eye is genuinely good — amber iris, round pupil, dark rim. Nobody would swap this head with another in the batch, but they would call it a striped anteater or a small theropod, not a hyena.
rows.topDefect: The heavy blunt hyena muzzle is drawn as a long needle snout and the two big pointed ears as one central cone, so the head reads as an anteater's — and the back stays level instead of sloping steeply from high shoulders to low hips.

rows.headWhy: The only masked face in the batch: a dark brow/eye patch over a large pale-iris eye, a small round ear tucked behind, and a short tapering muzzle with a tiny nose pad. That combination is not repeated elsewhere here, so it would not swap unnoticed. But the eye is a pale-iris eye inside a dark patch rather than the huge black eye the species is defined by, and the facial stripe stops at the brow instead of running to the nose.
rows.topDefect: There is no patagium and no long bushy tail — the animal is rendered as a small standing hoofed quadruped on four tube legs with a short bristle fan for a tail, so the two traits that make it a glider are simply absent.

rows.headWhy: Interchangeable with the Tasmanian Devil in this same batch — identical construction: dark rounded skull, one flat round ear drawn as a disc SUNK INTO the silhouette (reads as a socket, not a protruding ear), a small white-ringed eye with a round pupil in the same position, and a stubby blunt muzzle with a tiny dark nose bead. The only difference is that this muzzle is a few pixels longer and paler. Nothing about it says bear rather than marsupial.
rows.topDefect: The head is the same generic dark round-eared skull the Tasmanian Devil in this batch wears, and the body carries none of the species markers — no golden-cream chest crescent, no long curved climbing claws, and hoof-like feet instead of flat plantigrade bear paws.

rows.headWhy: The underlying head is a featureless tan goat skull identical in build to the Takin's — same long muzzle wedge, same absent ear, same pale-hook horn treatment. The horn is a thick cream C drawn as a FLAT decal lying on top of the face, emerging from the cheek rather than the top of the skull, and it curls forward and down over the muzzle instead of back and down. Worse, the eye is a solid dark-brown blob with no iris, no pupil and no lid — the one feature that could individuate the head has been left blank and half-buried under the horn.
rows.topDefect: The horns are a flat pale hook pasted across the cheek and muzzle rather than short thick horns rising from the skull and curving back and down, and they occlude a face whose eye is only an unstructured brown blob.

rows.headWhy: Same construction as the Tahr: a pale ring/hook horn lying flat over the cheek, a brown wedge with a single white nick for an eye, no readable ear, and a long pale muzzle. Coat hue is the main thing separating the two heads. The muzzle does have some Roman arch and a marked nostril, which is the one genuinely takin-specific note, but it is not enough to survive a swap.
rows.topDefect: The horns are a flat pale ring resting on the cheek instead of thick bosses sweeping outward then back from the crown, and the shaggy golden coat is rendered as a fringe of loose straw spikes poking out of a smooth barrel with no humped shoulder.

rows.headWhy: Distinct in this batch, but distinct as a pig: the muzzle terminates in a large flat pink disc with two round drilled nostrils — precisely the flat disc snout the reference forbids — with no droop, no mobility and no proboscis taper. The eye is one of the better ones here (amber iris, round pupil, white catchlight). The ears are two small dark downward-pointing triangles sitting low on the cheek beside the eye, so they read as face markings rather than the high rounded ears a tapir has, and a detached grey tube hangs below the mouth line.
rows.topDefect: The snout is a flat pink pig disc with two round nostrils instead of a short mobile proboscis, so the render lands on exactly the misread the reference explicitly warns against.

rows.headWhy: Swappable with the Sun Bear in this batch without anyone noticing — same dark rounded skull, same sunken round ear disc, same white-ringed round-pupil eye at the same height, same tiny blunt nose nub. It is a small round bear head. There is no oversized blocky braincase, no wide gape, no heavy jaw musculature, and no whisker or lip structure to mark it as a carnivorous marsupial.
rows.topDefect: The head is small, round and identical to the Sun Bear's instead of the oversized blocky skull with gaping jaws that defines the species — and the white chest band is missing while the tail is a thin curled hook rather than a thick tapering one.

rows.headWhy: Distinguishable in-batch — it is the only head with no ear at all and a very long, thin, downward-tapering snout ending in a pin-sized nose dot, with a fine lip line running its whole length. But that specificity is the WRONG species: a sloth has a short, flat, round face with a blunt nose and dark eye patches. This head reads as an anteater or an opossum. The eye is a correct ringed iris with a round pupil, but it sits high on a domed cranium no sloth has.
rows.topDefect: The animal has no claws whatsoever — the four straight tube legs end in tiny two-toe caps — and the long beaked snout makes it read as an anteater standing on a lawn rather than a flat-faced sloth.

rows.headWhy: Interchangeable with the Spectacled Bear in this batch: identical dark domed skull, identical flat round ear pasted on as a hard-edged disc with a concentric inner ring, identical tapering snout with a bulbous dark nose pad, identical small white-ringed eye. The only difference is a slightly brighter eye ring. Nothing says sloth bear — the snout should be PALE grey and mobile, but it is the same dark tone as the skull, and a stray line crosses the cheek like a misplaced whisker.
rows.topDefect: The coat is a pale grey striped barrel with straggly straw sticking out of the silhouette, not a shaggy black coat with a shoulder mane and a pale chest blaze — the dark head sits on a light body like two different animals joined.

rows.headWhy: The yellow eye with a hard vertical slit pupil is unmistakable and the only one in the batch; the muzzle is genuinely short and blunt with a domed skull, which is right for this cat. But the ear is the same flat pasted grey disc the bears wear, and it is placed just above and behind the eye at nearly eye size with a pink inner ellipse — so the head reads as having two eyes, one blank.
rows.topDefect: The single most iconic trait is absent: instead of an enormously long thick ropy tail there is a short white club with a fan of straight black bristles radiating from it, reading as a hairbrush stuck to the rump.

rows.headWhy: Swappable with the Sloth Bear without anyone noticing — same dark dome, same disc ear, same tapered snout and nose pad, same ringed eye. The pale eye ring that should be the whole point is only a thin bright circle at the eye rim, too small to read as a spectacle marking at normal size, and there is no second ring or chest extension.
rows.topDefect: The body is a pale grey-brown barrel on four jointless tubes with a solid dark disc on the hip, so the blackish shaggy bear mass never arrives and the dark head looks bolted onto a different creature.

rows.headWhy: In-batch it is separable by the dark triangular ear and the amber round-pupil eye, but the specificity is wrong: a spotted hyena has large ROUNDED ears and this is a sharp folded triangle with a hard notch. Below the ear the head is the same tan tapering tube-muzzle the Springbok wears — no bulging masseter, no heavy jowl, no blunt bear-like snout. It reads jackal, not hyena.
rows.topDefect: The defining silhouette is missing — the topline is nearly level with no high shoulders sloping down to low hips, and the forelimbs are the same length as the hind ones, so the animal reads as a spotted pony.

rows.headWhy: The horns and the brown brow band separate it in-batch, but remove the horns and the head is the same tan tapered muzzle with a nose dot and a lip line as the hyena's. Worse, there are NO EARS at all — a springbok's long leaf ears are one of its loudest features and only a small brown lump sits behind the horn base. There is no white face and no dark eye-to-nose stripe; the eye is a grey bead rather than the large dark eye the row calls prominent.
rows.topDefect: The horns are two smooth, pale, unringed rubbery prongs drawn as a symmetric U hooking forward, instead of black ringed lyre horns curving IN at the tips — and with no side stripe and no white belly the whole animal is a single flat tan.
